analysis.one_liner: Lets private employers pay overtime as time off instead of cash, at the employee's option.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2017 with 22 Senate cosponsors and died in the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, employers must pay hourly workers 1.5 times their wage for overtime hours, in cash. This bill would let private employers offer time off instead — 1.5 hours off for each overtime hour — if the employee agrees in writing. Unused time would have to be paid out in cash by January 31 of the next year, or when the employee quits, is fired, or asks in writing. The bill caps banked time at 160 hours, bars employers from pressuring workers to choose time off, and expires after five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of hourly workers gain the most: they could shift overtime compensation from a guaranteed cash payment to time off they control the scheduling of, and hold the cash until the end of the year, the equivalent of an interest-free loan. Some workers with predictable schedules and family demands could genuinely benefit from banking 1.5 hours of time off per overtime hour — but only if their employer offers the option and lets them use it.

how_it_helps.text: Employees who agree could bank one and a half hours of paid time off for every overtime hour worked, rather than receiving the overtime in cash.
Employees could withdraw the agreement at any time and could ask in writing for cash payment of banked time, which the employer would owe within 30 days.
Banked time would be paid in cash at the higher of the regular rate when earned or the final regular rate, on job loss or by January 31 of the following year.
Employers would be barred from intimidating, threatening, or coercing employees over the choice, with double damages for violations.

analysis.who_pays: Hourly overtime workers bear the risk: their overtime shifts from guaranteed cash in their paycheck to time off that the employer can refuse to schedule if it would 'unduly disrupt' operations. Workers who never get to use the banked time effectively lend their overtime wages to the employer for up to a year, interest-free, until the mandatory January 31 payout.

drawbacks.text: An employer must let an employee use requested time off only if it does not 'unduly disrupt the operations of the employer' — so the employer, not the worker, decides when banked time is actually taken.

The bill lets employers offer comp time only under a collective bargaining agreement or an individual agreement, which gives employers in non-union workplaces an incentive to press workers into signing, even though the bill bans making it a condition of employment.
Because the bill allows an employer to discontinue a comp time policy on 30 days' notice, an employer could pivot in and out of the system as its cash-flow needs change.

The anti-coercion rule relies on employees proving intimidation after the fact; the bill's own remedies run through complaints and Labor Department enforcement rather than blocking the practice up front.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for a worker with a predictable job and family obligations is real: banking time at a 1.5 rate can be worth more than the cash. The problem is the balance of power around that choice. In a non-union workplace the employer writes the agreement, controls scheduling of the time off through the 'undue disruption' exception, and holds the cash for up to a year — so the worker's 'option' depends on the same employer who benefits from not paying cash. Whether the safeguards hold would depend heavily on enforcement, which the bill asks the Government Accountability Office to study but does not strengthen beyond double damages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the bill in the Senate on April 3, 2017.
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Twenty-two senators cosponsored the bill: 21 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
No further action was ever recorded; the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Overtime protections stayed exactly as they were: hourly workers kept the guarantee of cash overtime, and employers did not gain the option of paying overtime in time off. Nothing changed for anyone, but the parties that pushed the bill got no new advantage either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no one gained

sides.party_line_note: The 22 cosponsors split 21 Republicans to 1 Democrat (Sen. Tom Udall of New Mexico), and the bill never advanced past its Republican-controlled committee of referral.

industries.industry: Employers of hourly overtime workers (retail, restaurants, logistics, services)
industries.note: The bill would let these employers pay overtime in time off rather than cash, hold that cash until January 31, and control when banked time is used. The savings and scheduling flexibility flow to the employer; the risk of never getting paid or never getting the time falls on the worker.

Union-negotiated overtime pay is cash by default, and unions opposed letting individual agreements substitute employer-controlled time off, viewing it as erosion of the Fair Labor Standards Act's cash guarantee. The bill would permit comp time through collective bargaining agreements, but only on terms unions would have to bargain for.

A new category of paid time off would require new tracking, written agreements, and annual payout systems — new business for firms that sell payroll and timekeeping compliance. Workers would see no direct effect.
